By Megumi Kaizu

The exhibition “Two Home Countries” was exhibited at Japan Society from September 12th, 2025 through January 11th, 2026.

The first New York solo museum exhibition of contemporary Japanese artist Chiharu Shiota, “Two Home Countries” consists of her site-specific and immersive works created to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II. Shiota works with themes common across her oeuvre such as memory, time, space, the body and blood. In conjunction with the launch of her exhibition, Shiota’s stage design was featured through the Society’s new theater commission this fall. Based on Yukio Mishima’s The Temple of the Golden Pavilion (1956) , the exhibition showcases Shiota’s intimate stage design work to American audiences for the first time. The commissioned play Kinkakuji marked the 100th year anniversary of Mishima’s birth with a series of four programs based upon his works. Kinkakuji is a Zen Buddhist temple originally built in 1397, but the current pavilion was rebuilt in 1955 after an arson attack.

In the first gallery, there is a 28-minute videorecording of her interview “The Chronology of Chiharu Shiota” (2024), in which Shiota discusses her recollections about relocating to Germany, studying with Marina Abramovic, missing Japan, moving very frequently in Germany, her life in East Berlin, etc. She recounts how all the experiences influenced her artmaking, reflecting on her self-consciousness about being a Japanese in Germany, mentioning how she never thought much about her identity as a Japanese person living in Japan. Through this shifting experience and perspective, she developed the idea of skin as a “dress” as a means of reflecting upon her experience of body and identity. In different ways, both Shiota and Mishima worked with themes of the body and sense of self, and I found their shared themes and interests intriguing. Mishima was an avid martial artist and also published a photo book of his images, as well as appearing in 6 movies. Image-making and performance art were the mediums that the two artists were interested in. In addition to Shiota’s 2024 interview, visitors can watch three recordings of her performance art pieces in the exhibition.

In her mixed media installation “Diary” (2025), Shiota explores an expansive record of shared human existence across national boundaries by weaving together copies of diaries written by Japanese soldiers and German civilians. She is drawn to the intimacy of diary-keeping, collecting handwritten pages that recount profoundly personal experiences. Shiota refers to the work of a Japanese scholar Donald Keene who was tasked to read and translate Japanese soldiers’ blood-stained diaries left on the battlefield when he was a US intelligence officer during WWII. She states that she drew on Keene’s experience to highlight the sense of memory and existence in absence by featuring pages of personal diaries in a web of connections. She reflects on fallen Japanese soldiers and, through this, explores her own personal struggles with issues such as identity, loss and nationhood. Strands of red yarn seem to become connective webs that resemble blood vessels or neurons in the human brain. The Japanese soldiers’ diaries were paired or juxtaposed with German civilians’ post-war writings. I found it somewhat challenging to interpret the soldiers’ writings in “Diary” because various aspects of the Pacific War continue to be controversial. I also thought it was an interesting choice for Shiota to present the Japanese soldiers' writings with the post-war writings of German civilians. On one level, I felt that Japan and Germany were her “two home countries”, making the choice of pairing relatable. On another level, as visitors view her work in New York, it appears elusive as to what her intentions might have been as an artist based in Germany. Walking through the large-scale installation made with red yarn and war-themed writing is a both immersive and hallowing experience. Its labyrinth-like appearance made me think of the intricacy and opaqueness of her aesthetic choices and intentions. "Diary” also made me think of Mishima’s “Sun and Steel,” in which the author explores his memories, thoughts and feelings of years both during and after WWII. Similarly, readers may find some of Mishima’s ideas in “Sun and Steel” challenging especially around World War II and suicide attacks. His language is layered and not always straightforward, sounding allegorical and metaphorical in many instances. He mentions the works of Romantic writers such as Yates and Novalis, as he discusses the subjects of body and language, which suggests the enduring impact Romanticism had on his early and later work, including The Temple of the Golden Pavilion.

In the second gallery, Shiota’s concept drawings are projected onto white cords in the manner of the performance of a theatrical adaptation of Mishima’s novel The Temple of the Golden Pavillion. There is also a video projection of stage highlights of the play Kinkakuji (2025) commissioned to celebrate the centennial of Mishima’s birth. Visitors can view Shiota’s flexible stage design for Kinkakuji made with numerous cords suspended from a large grid filling the stage space. The lit cords appear elegant and minimalistic while having a quality of entanglement, connecting further to “Diary.” The novel explores a fictionalized account of the monk who burned down Kinkakuji in 1950. The withdrawn protagonist chronicles his life as a narrator, discussing his earlier recollections and growing obsession with Kinkakuji as the most beautiful object in the world, revealing his thoughts and feelings toward beauty. Shiota’s sketches (water-soluble wax pastel, watercolor, ink and pencil on paper) made during rehearsals of Kinkakuji give viewers a glimpse into her working process.

The last gallery presents Shiota’s drawings and videos alongside her large-scale art installation. All the pieces in the room share such themes as home, the body, space and illness. The 2025 installation “Two Home Countries” (metal frame, wire, rope and beads) allows viewers to explore her thoughts and feelings toward Japan and Germany as her two home countries. There is the recurring use of red yarn, building the connective web between all installations. In some sense, I felt that history, including warfare and collective memories and trauma, connects the two countries for Shiota who experiences an “awakening longing” for a place where she is not. The two houses in the installation are separated by wave-like shapes made with red yarn, suggesting that there is some space like a sea that separates her two homes, reminding viewers that it is impossible to be physically present in two separate places. What’s left might only be a sense of longing.

Shiota went through cancer treatment and the themes of pain, death and fear echo in pieces such as “Cell”. The themes of body and pain are also present in Mishima’s works, albeit from different standpoints and experiences. World War II casts a strong, lasting shadow on Mishima’s works such as “Sun and Steel” and “The Temple of the Golden Pavillion.” Shiota’s “Cell,” made of glass, key and thread, caught my attention as it is visually striking and poignant. The narrator of the Temple of the Golden Pavillion mentions a rusty key as an analogy for his speech impairment which causes communication issues and impacts his self-image and sense of self. Shiota’s concept of dress and artistic preoccupation with the body and skin demonstrate timeless themes––namely, alienation, nationality, memory, the body and pain––that endure throughout the works of both artists.

“The trouble with socialism,” Oscar Wilde quipped, “is that it takes up too many evenings.” Much the same can be said for organizing, and conferences about organizing. Who has the evenings, much less the afternoons and the mornings, to dedicate to what’s most needful in our lives? To have the one-on-ones; to attend the endless meetings? To form the splinter-cell, the grouposcule or caucus? To think deeply (and soulfully) while in boisterous assembly?

The Student Movements and Social Justice: Histories and Futures conference took place Tuesday, March 10, between 9.30 a.m. and 5.00 p.m., bringing activists and theorists from across the globe into Elebash Hall for a long recitation of our current contradictions. In the span of one roundtable, a Quebecois comrade made the case for long-term trust-building (“If you spend 50 years respecting the rules, then they will respect when the strike passes”), while a South African veteran of the Fees Must Fall movement argued that the point is not to “win the space, but build the space.” Whether wedded to a staid unionism or a more experimental approach, those attending the conference all agreed on two things. One, that contradictions abound, and that we must deal with critical difference such that it becomes a resource rather than a weakness. Two, that Palestine should be our compass today. A talk on the latter, the keynote entitled “Sumud in the Face of Scholasticide,” furnished the conference its most plangent note: Do not be complicit. Much of the debate focused on how to do this.

Some seemed to consider longer, more capacious meetings as the best strategic option given our dire straits. They outlined plenary spaces with a baroque floorplan: decision plenaries, education plenaries, public-facing plenaries. (Organizing begets more organizing; see Wilde above.) Is this what Marx meant by “free association of producers”? “What Minneapolis needed after all that mutual aid organizing,” one attendee said at coffee hour, “was to develop soviets.” A good point but easier said than done. As for the university as a site of struggle, an ingenious idea came about during the section entitled “Abolitionist University”: Nationalize the private endowments. At first it sounded ultra and maximalist. But then, returning to the asbestos-ridden corridors of CUNY, it began to seem not only reasonable but necessary.

A packed room, a rallying "Fuck ICE" to kick things off.

Speaking of "what's most needful in our lives," The Left Voice and the GC Immigrant Solidarity Working Group put on a memorable evening that featured moving firsthand accounts from the Twin Cities on how to fight back against ICE.

Amid the constant hubbub of ever-more-depressing news, one would almost forget that the start of 2026 was marked by a historic standoff between the Minnesota working-class and the Trump's administration would-be Praetorian Guard.

Three members of Left Voice, present on the ground in January, testified to the violence, but also to the wave of solidarity that took hold in the onslaught. They reminded the audience that, even though the intensive ICE crackdown in Minneapolis ended on February 12, 2026, the Twin cities are still occupied today. As of late February, a dozen abductions a day were still counted, according to R., the most profoundly affecting witness.

Her testimony really stood out for its sense of drama and sacrifice. Live on Zoom from Minneapolis, R., a teacher committed to protecting her students and their families, gave us a glimpse into her daily life and that of thousands of others in the war on Minneapolis. Against the backdrop of a long legacy of police brutality, she spoke of the community of protesters of which she is a part—teachers, labor organizers, activists. She recounted how mutual aid groups, originally set up during the pandemic, were reactivated to provide families with life's essentials. She described how people delivering supplies were advised not to operate alone, and how their licence plates were recorded by ICE.

Tears, tissues, warm applause.

If one had to take a single lesson from the evening, it is that Minneapolis proved to us that ICE is not untouchable.

Running into an English PhD from Stanford at a cafe, this dispatcher was reminded of the low conditions we are forced to endure as CUNY grad workers. Discoursing on her teaching load, how some of her classes held as few as three students, the Stanford PhD balked when she was told how early in the program we teach, how often and how many students comprise our class load. “But how do you get anything done?” she asked, almost pleading on our behalf. And when she heard of our fifth year cut-off in funding—and the wintertime ordeal of fellowship-hunting— she nearly fell out of her chair.

Fellowship season has become far more bleak in the last couple years. After the Writing Across the Curriculum fellowship (WAC) was scrapped in 2024, the scramble for financial support for 6+years in the humanities has taken place under conditions of increased scarcity. Application pools have grown exorbitant while fellowship opportunities remain paltry. What’s more, from the position of academic development, most of these fellowships are useless. Peruse any of the “opportunities” on offer and you will notice a worrisome tilt towards the administrative. I won’t add any specifics here, but you can fill in your own rollcall of job-descriptions: all those “collaborative work environments” that require graduates to perform bureaucratic busywork while feeding on the pap of “professionalization” and 30k a year instead of working on their research. And this after multiple rounds of interviews, sometimes group interviews where we are asked to perform “collaboration” in conditions of the most debased competition. But hey, at least there’s health insurance!

Taking all this in, the Stanford PhD asked if I had ever read Invisible Man. I replied I hadn’t since high school and she counselled me to check out the first chapter.

On March 13, 2026, Dr. Shannon Mattern, Director of Creative Research at Metropolitan New York Library Council, gave an expansive presentation on the concept of the index in our current epistemological, political and ecological context, as a part of the Spring 2026 Friends of the Mina Rees Library Luncheon. Entitled Pointing at Clouds: Indexing, Searching, and Citing in an Age of AI Smog, the presentation was a tour-de-force of Derridean wordplay, impassioned ethical commitment, and convivial collaborative spirit that ought to be expected from engaged and critical academic work. Mattern began her presentation in our immediate situation—“the cloud,” a term of art for third-party digital storage, has been outed as “a gauzy euphemism” for the ruthless extraction of natural resources in the name of heightened surveillance and policing. As a Creative Index resident at the Cooper-Hewitt Museum, she sought “to peer through the fog and find some stabilizing order,” approaching the index not merely as “a bibliographic convention, or an organizational method, or a media form, or a financial instrument, or a corporeal component,” but also as “an intellectual architecture, a literary genre, a creative form, a semiotic concept, and an embodiment of agency.”

While seeking this expanded territory for the index, her language consistently embodied the form of its object; pointing toward a future in which the trace and its source were brought into harmony. “Indexes, then, are caused by, and serve as evidence or traces of, or they designate the existence of, the things they represent.” This became most evident when the act of indexing was made literal through the tactile arts, considering fingers themselves as “indexes of agency and signaling tools,” as well as a tool with which to “register refusal” of AI. In this collapsing of the object and its referent into the hand, I sensed an impending storm. Mattern’s noble performance of linguistic and conceptual dexterity was culminating in a call for greater “attunement to place,” indexing as the display of indigenous “knowledges…germinated by their contexts, born of the soil and clouds,” forms of intelligence “that need to be experienced in their full, situated materiality, observed and appraised through sensitivities cultivated across generations.”

In this fervent defense of premodern epistemologies, the initial (and quite moving) mytheme of the cloud-as-knowledge was lost to a more basic, and problematic, enframing. Clouds are not localized, ancestral technologies. They are suspended particles that form under particular conditions. Following the path of a raindrop from the cloud, the presentation collapsed under its conceptual accumulation. The cloud was no longer the figure of emancipatory practice — forsaken for the trace of a raindrop, the trauma of the mark. If we are to take our cues from natural processes, we might do well to turn instead to the anarchic dérive, the happening, all that which makes itself untraceable in the play of anonymity. We are not clouds; we are clouds. A poem by the Sōtō Zen Buddhist monk, Ryōkan:

Relying upon a finger, we see the moon
Relying upon the moon, we understand the finger.
Moon and finger
Are neither the same nor different.
This expedient analogy is for guiding beginners.
Having seen reality as it is,
There is neither moon nor finger.

Student newspaper evokes cloying undergrads and an extracurricular for the unathletic. It's difficult—at least for me—to understand it as any kind of center, a place for anyone to turn in order to ground their understanding of a school. Perhaps it’s because the qualifier “student” is one that tacitly denigrates the entity “newspaper”—perhaps like how, for many in the United States, “public” is a qualifier that denigrates the entity “school.”

However I like to think that our school, which positions itself as a graduate center of the sprawling CUNY system, isn’t quite so terrified of the trivial. Not because we ourselves are trivial, but because we are faced with a set of challenges that keep us teetering ever on the edge of the absurd (do insiders not speak of CUNY as if it were an eccentric uncle of sorts?). We graduate students are situated in a former department store staring down the Empire State Building; we are dispatched everywhere from Staten Island to the Upper East Side, shouldering a hefty dose of pedagogical labor, frequently underresourced. We are not even so much a college as a center in a “university” that is, in truth, 25 campuses integrated into the seething organism that is New York City. We search for unity, things fall apart. Can the center hold?

The mistake that I often see is treating CUNY–or particularly the Graduate Center– as an upwards striver, sitting just an arm's reach from the Ivies. Au contraire. You have to love CUNY for its absurdities and be radicalized by its failures. In order to believe that “public” does not denigrate “university,” we at the GC ought to celebrate being the public, the popular, the front lines of struggle.

So it goes with “student” in relation to “newspaper.” In 1996, the Advocate, then 7 years old and inscribed on newsprint, won the campus alternative journalism award for anti-racist journalism and outstanding investigative reporting. At the time the Advocate came out often–roughly every other month–and fulfilled numerous functions that have since been superseded by digital media. But besides that, it served a meaningful centering function that doesn't seem obsolete. They tagged themselves “the voice of the Graduate Center,” with the implication–much harder to grasp in today’s media landscape–that a collective, univocal cry might be a good course towards being heard.

Since February, I have been digitizing all issues of the Advocate going back to its founding for the CUNY Digital History Archive. It’s given me a lot of time with the magazine, speeding through years splashed across yellowing pages. Taken in total, the collection offers a compelling history of the Graduate Center as reflexively progressive and hotly engaged in social issues. Amidst the CUNY budget crisis of 1995-1996, which saw governor Pataki cut nearly $100 million in allocations to CUNY, the chancellor declared a state of financial exigency, and demanded capitulation from Grad Center administration. In such situations of retrenchment, the sentiment of “it has to be this way” trickles down from the highest reaches. The result is something like the New York Times tendency to say things like “bombs dropped in Gaza” and “hundreds die in explosion,” situating the source of said bombs alongside that pesky “it” who makes it rainy, warm, nighttime, late, and so forth. The writers for the Advocate over those years had an itinerant drive to put names and faces to the failures, to hold power to account. As a historical document, it stands as a counter to the master narrative, showing skepticism and resistance to institutional buck passing.

Advocating for change calls for an obsessive personality, an almost pitiless sense that there is more to be done. Part of the iterative quality is not just the slow weight of change or the heft of resistance, but also the work to keep certain struggles on peoples’ minds. I guess that’s why this particular student newspaper came to call itself the Advocate (despite the name already belonging to a longstanding gay magazine). The Graduate Center’s paper exists not as a chronicle, a herald, a post, a times, nor a tribune, but as an advocate, a force of advocating. The Advocate then is best when it's a prosthesis, a student voice made solid–or, rather, a collection of student voices carried as one, lifting some part of the iterative burden off each speaker. If there is any future for the Advocate in an age of fast media, it’s as a source of solidity, of grounding, of containing and carrying precisely what threatens to dissipate but must stick around.

As I sat to write these words, I couldn’t help but reflect on what had happened to me the day before, in Mannheim, Germany, where kids were making monkey noises in my direction. In these moments of absolute incredulity, the immediate reaction tends to be to question your senses. Standing there, fumbling the keys to the apartment where I was staying, I wondered if I had undergone a bout of daydreaming. But “ou-ou-ah-ah” seems a universal enunciation of monkey noises, breaking any language barrier. Moreover, the kids, probably no more than six or seven years old, rushing to hide behind the gated barrier, seemed to confirm what my ears had sensed.

These instances of overt racism tend to offer a springboard to look back home, where the familiar surroundings ostensibly form a bulwark to sustain any aggression. James Baldwin, from the tiny Swiss village of Leukerbad was able to reflect on his strangeness there, as opposed to his familiar perilousness as a Black man at home. He sees “a dreadful abyss between the streets of this village and the streets of the city in which I was born, between the children who shout Neger! today and those who shouted Nigger! yesterday—the abyss is experience, the American experience.” Because of the lack of history, lack of presence of Black people in that Swiss town, Baldwin was ready to accept a lack of malevolence on the part of the children, to grant them some moral leeway that he might not have granted to those that shouted that epithet in the United States.

This digression into Mannheim and Leukerbad serves only to highlight a few incidents that may often be portrayed as isolated. We may tend to think that this experience simply reflects Europe’s unwillingness to reconcile with the presence of Black people in their midst. Baldwin certainly attributed his experience with that line of thinking: “The black man, as a man, did not exist for Europe. But in America, even as a slave, he was an inescapable part of the general social fabric and no American could escape having an attitude toward him.” As true as this is, and as much as there is work to do on the subject of recognizing the Black (or non-white) presence in Europe, this may isolate issues that are evidence of a lingering problem.

Baldwin opened his essay by stating: “From all available evidence no black man had ever set foot in this tiny Swiss village before I came.” In my case, there is ample evidence of the presence of non-white people in Mannheim. Fifty percent of people living there have a migration background; they are primarily of Turkish provenance (as the largest minority group in Germany there is an extensive history of anti-Turkish racism). Therefore, I cannot blame my experience on some lack of contact with the foreigner. I rack my head for influences the children at the gate may have had: parents, social media, a society that still harbors and normalizes daily microaggressions. Presence alone does not suffice to correct this, as the US has shown.

If we turn closer to home, we may tend to think we’re past that sort of crude racism. Many would like to think we are. Seventy-three years have passed since Baldwin’s “Stranger in the Village” essay and the last few key figures of the Civil Rights movement are slowly dying. But it might be fair to pause and wonder how much today’s world matches the re-imagining of American society that Baldwin had envisioned. Because when Allyson Friedman, a professor employed at Hunter, expresses “They’re too dumb to know they’re in a bad school” at a moment when she might have presumed that no one can hear—at a moment when a Black student was speaking—easy visions of having moved past our worst moments of race relations slowly dissolve.

Yet, there may still be an inclination to flag this as an aberration, an isolated incident. Hunter’s communication was quick to note that the “remarks were made in the individual’s role as a private citizen.” True, and probably important legally. But for a student’s understanding, who’s to say where the line between private citizen and university professor begins? Michael Levin, professor emeritus at CCNY has published on racial differences in intelligence, claiming that Black people’s lower IQ means that their lower representation on philosophy faculties is fair. This is unlike Friedman’s comment as it is published expressly for people to read, hear about and perhaps be contentious about. But it’s eerily similar in its steadfast attack on Black intelligence.

Then the LORD God formed a man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being.
Genesis 2:7.

I am the sun of the Earth.
Earthly flight.
Buried vermin and debris.
Flower bites and animal smells.
The scent of desire is in the branches of the trees.
Memories are dewdrops.
The Earth is a torn manuscript.
The cheerful grasses cry out.
The summer foliage is so frivolous.

The jealous sun has lost its virility in the face
Of the earth desecrated by our transgressions,
Our unbridled pleasures and jubilations.
Life is a disastrous love affair.
Time is silent like a grenade on the ground.
The clock is a sword of Damocles;
It will strike the hour of the harvest.

All human passions are childish illusions.
The earth straddled is tattooed with dreams and drifts.
It speaks to me under hypnosis of its suicidal anxieties.
The towers of this famous city are its breasts
Taut and pointed like the peak of a proud mountain.

What does the earth do to life?
What does life do to the earth?
What do living beings do to the earth?
What do they do with the Earth?
What does the Earth do and undo?
The terrestrial is terrible, fatal.
Is Earth a planet of hell or paradise?
Are we drunk with life or death?
Die to live or live to die?
Must we be drunk to live or to die?
The questions of ferns and wild anemones.
The irony of volcanic lava, silent and noisy disasters!

Love is a slow chaos.
Flowers cry like virgin girls.
The whole earth is sacrificed and sold at auction.
Everything explodes!
Is loving the Earth like holding a time bomb close to your heart?
The ground is a minefield.
The future is a volcano.
Distress. Storms. Devastation. Crises.

Landscapes erased from my memory as a rejected lover.
I love you like one plunges into hell.
The ground is our open grave.
What is earth care?
Who sold the soul of the Earth?
Who can (still) save the Earth?
Can the Earth save us?
Can the Earth speak?

Capitalism is a tragedy, a dance of death.
All masks will fall like the stripped, violated, and emptied earth.
Violence weighs heavier than all the towers in the world.
Am I David? Who is Goliath?
Has God turned his back on the Earth?

Paradise will emerge from the Earth's womb,
Stretched out like a futuristic sex organ.
The ecstasy of Eden lies at the bottom of the Earth.
All trees enjoy flowering.
Everything that rots has laughed for a long time.
Mud is the Earth's seminal gold.
We are dust.

Armel J. Ngamaleu

I’ll present to poems in translation, by writers persecuted whom the Nazis persecuted.

Exile had a special meaning for Else Lasker-Schüler (1869-1945). Early during her career, the Jewish German expressionist poet began referring to herself as “Joseph of Thebes” and “Prince Yussuf of Egypt”. The Biblical reference to the favourite son of Israel who was sold into Egyptian slavery by his brothers, served as a symbol of galut: the Jewish existence in diaspora. In 1933, Else Lasker-Schüler managed to leave Germany for Switzerland, where, however, she was barred from publishing or working. After her third journey to Palestine in 1939, she, by now stateless, was refused a return visa by the Swiss authorities. She lived in the relatively small German-speaking Jewish community of Jerusalem, where she wrote this poem:

Mein blaues Klavier

Ich habe zu Hause ein blaues Klavier

Und kenne doch keine Note.

Es steht im Dunkel der Kellertür,

Seitdem die Welt verrohte.

Es spielten Sternenhände vier –

Die Mondfrau sang im Boote.

– Nun tanzen die Ratten im Geklirr.

Zerbrochen ist die Klaviatur.

Ich beweine die blaue Tote.

Ach liebe Engel öffnet mir

– Ich aß vom bitteren Brote –

Mir lebend schon die Himmelstür,

Auch wider dem Verbote.

My blue piano

I have got a sky-blue piano at home,

Yet know not one singular note.

It stands ‘mid dark cellar-doors’ stone,

Since all the world’s turnèd cutthroat.

Once, star-hands’ play; four brightly shone -

The moon-wife would sing from her boat.

Now rats dance ‘mong clattering bone.

The claviature has been smote.

Her sky-like blue corpse I bemoan.

O open for me --- dear angels, ye mote,

The bitter-bread's taste I have known ---

Alive, that heaven’s gate high afloat,

And if it’s against the prohibitìon.

The poem presents difficult challenges to the translator. The meter is a mix of iambs (da-DA) and anapests (da-da-DA), with every line beginning with an iamb. In German, as in English poetry, iambs are often used as a “default” meter. The anapest can be used for jaunty, high-spirited rhymes; in this poem, it has an uncanny, estranging effect. Anapests are easier to achieve in German, which has plenty of adjectival and verbal endings, than in English. In order to reproduce some of the German anapests in English, I, for example, chose to translate “blaues” (‘blue’) as “sky-blue”. This translation also anticipates the “heavenly gate” of the last stanza.

Additionally, the whole poem only uses two rhymes: AB AB ABA AB ABAB. In order to find matching rhyme-words in English, I slightly adjusted the schema: AB AB ABA BA BABA. I also made use of archaic language, viz. “smote” and “ye mote”. I hope that such KJV-like language is licensed by Lasker-Schüler’s own Biblical allusions, including to the “bitter bread” of exile.

In the last line, I introduce an ambiguity of pronunciation. “Prohibition” may be read in the ordinary, modern way: /proh-uh-BIH-shun/, but also in Victorian fashion, which is still preserved in Anglican hymns: /proh-uh-BIH-s(h)i-on/. The latter reading preserves the rhyme. While not in the original, I find the ambiguous resolution appealing.

Walter Benjamin (1892 - 1940) is remembered as a gnomic philosopher and social thinker, one of the founders of critical theory. However, throughout his life, he also wrote poetry: mostly sonnets, which recently have been translated into English. Already in 1931, he had moved to the then-isolated and remote island of Ibiza. He was trying to save money, or --- as he put it --- reduce his costs of living to the “European existence-minimum”. In September 1933, Benjamin left Ibiza for France; when the Germans conquered one half of the country and the remaining half surrendered to them under the rule of General Pétain’s regime at Vichy, Benjamin attempted to flee back to Spain over the Pyrenees. After the first attempt failed in Fall 1940, Benjamin, who was Jewish, took his own life. Shortly after the Nazis had taken power in Germany, he had written this (until now untranslated) piece in free verse:

Trauriges Gedicht

Man sitzt im Stuhle und schreibt.

Man wird müder und müder und müder.

Man legt sich zur richtigen Zeit,

Man isst zur richtigen Zeit.

Man hat Geld,

das hat der liebe Gott geschenkt.

Das Leben ist wunderbar!

Das Herz klopft lauter und lauter und lauter.

Das Meer wird stiller und stiller und stiller

bis auf den Grund.

San Antonio 11.3.33

Melancholy poem

One sits in the chair, and one writes.

One’s growing more tirèd and tirèd and tirèd.

One lies down at the right time.

And one eats at the right time.

One has money,

that’s the dear Lord’s gift.

And life is all wonderful!

The heart’s pounding louder and louder and louder,

The sea’s growing quieter ‘nd quieter ‘nd quieter,

down to the ground

San Antonio, 11.3.33

Like Lasker-Schüler's poem, Benjamin’s employs a combination of iambs and anapests. In my translation, I took care to preserve the meter, indicating that both “tirèd and” as well as “quieter ‘nd” should be read as trisyllabic. Benjamin clearly paid attention to the meter, as can be seen in his choosing the variant “Stuhle” over “Stuhl” in the first line.

Another challenge was presented by the German impersonal third-person pronoun “man”. I decided to go with a repetition of “one”. This is more stilted than the German, but it captures the detachment of the poem well. Replacing later instances of “one” with “he” or “they” would have failed to capture the original’s repetition. It would also have counter-acted a first-personal reading, which seems to be intended in the original.

“Not everybody seems to see the world they’re living in. It’s such a kick, really, seeing things.” —Lois Dodd

We all think we know red: the color of desire, the flowing hue of life. We may be familiar with the red of the pants of Manet’s The Fifer, or the tilted room of Matisse’s Red Studio (or Barnett Newman’s Vir Heroicus Sublimis, or that of Anne Carson’s Autobiography), but we don’t know red as Lois Dodd knows it. She’s a colorist; and the true colorists among us sense that color has a life of its own, that it requires new forms for each moment of its emergence. The red of noon. The red of late blossoming. The red of blood. The red of Lois Dodd on a fall day in 1977. We must see it as the colorist, feels it: anew.

Dodd’s is not the pure gesture of abstract expressionism, but rather a painting in which figural forms become self-reflexive vessels for color. Take the first two works in Lois Dodd: A Radiant Simplicity, the extensive exhibit recently held at the Art Gallery at Brooklyn College, where she taught for 20 years. They form a chronologically distant diptych: Red Maple, Blairstown (1998), Red Maple with Airplane (1997). In the first, the upper third of the canvas is dominated by a vermillion gash, a minimally textured block of paint on which a calligraphy of branches dance. The referent might well be a maple in autumnal bloom, but the red is the thing. In the second work, the vermillion grades scarlet and carmine and spreads across the entire canvas in dramatic jags, bolts of blue interjecting into the arrhythmic haze. The color has taken on a different character as we view the Red Maple from another angle (more vertiginous, from the tree’s undercarriage). Now, cobalt flashes: a revealed counterpoint of sky, the steel crucifix of a plane droning its silent note of elsewhereness and doom: and yet, red’s still the thing. Dodd’s choice of ordinary scenes affords her formal possibilities unavailable to abstract expressionism, and a pictorial intensity absent in referent-laden Pop Art.

This must be the exhibition’s radiant simplicity. The catalogue emphasizes Dodd’s own insistence on the pictorial and her close attendance to the before-her, the present, above all psychological or theoretical concerns. Lucy Lippard helpfully invokes cinema’s close-up (somehow Dreyer and Kiarostami combine here) to explain Dodd’s “complexity of simplicity.” Mona Hadler, author of the catalogue essay as well as one of the show’s curators, christens her an “abstract realist,” situating Dodd in post-war New York debates on abstraction and figuration (questions of representation that were often, to my mind, also about technological media; and whose Gordian knot was soon severed by Duchamp’s Telegram That Exploded, replacing the mimetic Idea of western art with the provisional concept of postmodernity). Mondrian informed her geometric renderings of the everyday, a refusal of depth that didn’t accede to pure Greenbergian “opticality,” offering Dodd a more grounded approach to post-war painting’s Great Flattening. Her muted visual flourish allowed for figurational depiction without regression to pre-modernist ideas, or submission to the photograph. The subtlety of her approach is stark when compared to the most well-known figure of the abstract realist style, Alex Katz. Whereas he went big and loud and autoreferential, Dodd opted for a more diminuendo approach: an “arresting stillness” produced by zeroing in on the motif.

Broken windows, unmonumental buildings, trees: these are some of Dodd’s motifs. While the thickness of her brushstroke lends itself less to the strong depth of Cézanne than the “shallow” depth of the postcubists, the paintings exhibit the same unrelenting concentration Cezanne lavished on his apples. (“He wanted true-to-life reproduction,” wrote DH Lawrence. “Only he wanted it more true to life.”) It would be a mistake to freight her paintings with phenomenological intentionality, however. Instead her objects, “carefully observed and simplified,” are distilled not to essence but absence. Over 48 works stretching between 1960 and 2025, it was the force of time that most weighed on the exhibition, the unapparent and paradoxical pressure of stillness that, by both moving and staying in one place, invites deformation. Failed instruments become thresholds, metaphors of the undercurrent: the broken window’s reflection is pocked by dark gaps like broken teeth (Broken Window, Maine, 1975); the cracked door, set aslant in its hold, is useless while closed yet obdurate to opening (Doorway at Blaisey’s Farm (nr. Van Campen’s Glen), 1991). On these thresholds, color seeps onto the deformed surface (that cadmium yellow in the window’s false azure…), while the door is thrown open to the unrepresentable, the felt, the half-known.

Dodd came up in the social democratic world of post-war New York City. She went to Cooper Union when it was free and when the center of the art world had just migrated from Paris. Kafka was the rage, rent was reasonable, and artists self-organized the 10th Street gallery scene, described by Dodd in the exhibition’s film as a replacement graduate program. With the galleries below and artist workspaces above, she was constantly in other people’s studios, studying the work, picking up ideas, leaving some of her own. This was the world of the journeyman artist in the downtown ‘50s: animated, artist-controlled, full of possibility.

There is an irony to an artist, who has taught in MFA programs, speaking preferentially of her non-academic tutelage; but such is the privilege of the old guard. We shouldn’t be too resentful to admit that the world that produced Dodd held more possibility than our own. It was a world of studio visits within an ecology of galleries that has now all but vanished, and with it the intensity that once buoyed the New York artworld. (“It was great,” grins Dodd. “People would get so excited about a painting they’d start beating each other up.”) Still, it's good to draw warmth from its afterglow, and to remind ourselves that every great style is the product of collective circumstances—of divvied rent and shared sensibilities. Moreover, it's somehow compensatory to acknowledge that if a painting is to “perspire with ecstasy” (as Henry Miller wrote in To Paint is to Love Again), it emerges from enthusiasms held in common, not the onanistic pleasures of the commodity.

As I walked around the Brooklyn College gallery, surrounded by the paintings, I wondered what I often wonder about the work of living artists—where do their paintings go, when they’re not in an exhibit? I imagined the vestibules of the rich, some of whom still share the touching magical belief that owning art confers power. I imagined the dust-strewn stacks in which the paintings are slotted like the cultural artifacts that they are and the textual memories they’ll become. Then there are the random interiors like my grandparents’ apartment, which happens to feature a Lois Dodd—she went to Cooper Union with my grandfather. On the back is written, with a blackened paintbrush, Red Maple in October, Dodd 1977. The red is dimmer in the living-room light, with greater hints of orange and water. The red also carpets the painting floor: falling leaves: a color to mark the passing of time: a close-up of red at its most luminous.

Interview by Souli Boutis

This April, the New Press reissued Joshua Freeman’s Working-Class New York on the occasion of its 25th anniversary. Though Professor Freeman, distinguished professor of history at the Graduate Center, seriocomically attributes this to the same windfall that all New York leftists received with the mayoral nomination of Zohran Mamdani, his book is a classic among readers of American labor history. Winner of the New York City Book Award in 2000, he himself has received the demotic title “dean of New York labor historians.” A hale, hearty septuagenarian with an old-school outer-boroughs accent (the word “broad” expanding with onomatopoeic gusto on his lips), his generosity suggested a man whose character matched the populism of his intellectual interests. His range of reference extended from Eric Hobsbawm to Bob Dylan, producing the unexpected revelation that the lyric “to live outside the law you must be honest” could be from Primitive Rebels as well as Blonde on Blonde. This all added to the surprising breadth of culture in the 340-ish pages of Working-Class New York: from Bernard Malamud to The Honeymooners, Freeman treats the reader to a suite of working-class production beyond the assembly-line and the forge. Besides a chronicle of the New York working-class’s triumph and confinement, the book tracks the “unusual worldliness” of the city’s proletariat at its post-war peak; the establishment of social democratic institutions by mid-century (some of which, like rent-stabilization, we still enjoy today); the extraordinary seizure of local strikes in the global crisis of the 70s; ending on a diagnosis of labor’s cultural disappearance in a portion titled, with sad premonition, “Trump City.” It remains unparalleled in its field for scope and depth.

What follows is a discussion of the period stretching between the end of the Second World War and the end of the 20th century in New York City, centering on what made New York a “labor town” and contributed to its eventual conversion into a “real estate state,” a process which has only accelerated in the 21st century.

In the “Preface to the 2026 Edition,” Freeman outlines some of the major transformations in the urban landscape since the millennium. Still dependent on its working class, now “larger and more diverse than ever,” its organized movement is less powerful than in the past. Between 1998 and 2025, manufacturing jobs fell from 190,800 to 54,400, even as the overall city workforce grew from 2.9 to 4.2 million. Employment in healthcare, during the same period, shot up from 452,600 to 1,037,000, while jobs in the FIRE economy (finance, insurance, real estate) and services swelled from 1.1 million to 1.4 million. The tech sector has grown the fastest, metamorphosing Manhattan’s West Side into that industry’s tawdry image of silicon glitz, while at the same time, one quarter of New Yorkers lived in poverty, double the national rate. By 2020, 37 percent of the population was foreign-born, with almost half of Queens born outside the United States. The unionization rate among foreign-born New Yorkers, in 2023-24, was higher than that among native-born, and the general level of union-membership, 19.8 percent of workers, was nearly double the national number. But this is down from one out of four workers in 2004. The consequences of all of this is a city that runs on “a vast army of low-paid workers,” often commuting from the cultural and linguistic cornucopias of the Bronx and Queens, while the cultural-economic character of Manhattan and parts of Brooklyn trend white, wealthy, and almost spiritually suburban. The global dynamics of core-periphery have been replicated in the metropole. The promise of Mamdani and the social forces that subtend him aside, the working class has ebbed in influence as well as power—and this redounds to the character of the city itself. In the words of the original “Introduction”: “As the working class has lost influence, New York has become a less civilized, more alienated community… So much of what made New York great came from their labor, their struggles, their jokes, and their songs. Forgetting that impoverishes us all.”

***

I'm guessing you're a New Yorker.

I was actually born in the Philadelphia area. My parents were New Yorkers who had moved there for various reasons, and then when I was a little kid, they moved back to New York. I grew up in Eastern Queens, way out on the border of Nassau County. We lived in a garden apartment, a subject on which I’ve recently become interested.

The spatial arrangement of New York, as the book points out, is quite different from the rest of America. Is that the reason for the city’s unusually high working class consciousness?

I'm a little reluctant to make too many comparative statements, but clearly population density in New York is very high by national standards. Car ownership is very low by national standards, and mass transit usage is very high. So by these basic markers, it's different. I think the neighborhood—and this is not unique to New York—but the neighborhood was a very important factor to working-class consciousness. And yet at the same time, because of cheap mass transit, the city was widely available. When I wrote this book in 2000, I wasn't thinking in terms of the “right to the city,” but mass transit makes the abstraction of the city real through democratic access. Neighborhoods could be provincial, but you had this kind of access, if you wanted it, to a very wide world.

You emphasize the cosmopolitanism, or “worldliness,” of the New York Working class.

There’s a dialectic at work here. I think some neighborhoods are more “worldly” than others, perhaps varying according to ethnicity. But ultimately, the very low level of home ownership always struck me as key in defining what New York is.

In the immediate aftermath of World War Two, the domestic balance of power shifted quite drastically from the preceding New Deal era. Under Truman, the Business Roundtable-types shaped a new “common sense” that made state economic planning, outside of the military, wholly impossible. New York seems to be an exception to that, and this can be traced to the power of organized labor in the city. You open the book with a panorama of strikes, which I read as an explicit rebuff to the revanche that took place after the Popular Front politics of WW2. Why start with the post-war strike wave?

It's the strongest and most visible display of class power. The extraordinary display of worker mobilization that you see in the first year or so after the war, is quite extraordinary by our current standards. And it illustrates how different the world was, how as a result of the Depression, the New Deal, the CIO and the war, you had an explicit class power that's rare in US history. And it's the “demonstration effect,” to use a social science term, that continues to shape politics in New York. I wanted to catch people's attention like, holy smokes, the whole city is shut down by these elevator operators and tugboat operators—people who are normally kind of invisible.

It is a very fluid moment—the five years or so after the war—because on one hand, clearly the left is defeated. The Cold War happens. And yet in funny ways, especially in New York, but not only in New York, a lot of the ideas that animated the left wing of the New Deal and the CIO continue to be highly influential in shaping the city, often in ways that are unacknowledged. Later on in the book, when I'm talking about housing, it's striking to me how very radical projects have these incredibly bland and meaningless names like Penn South.

Here, a union [the International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union] on the most expensive real estate in the world, builds this co-op so blue collar workers can walk to work—and it's called Penn South!

Not quite Red Vienna.

In some ways, much more impressive than Red Vienna. And yet it's not called Karl Marx Hoff, it's called Penn South.

That touches on an interesting dynamic in Working-Class New York. I saw it structured around a double-helix: One is the narrative of the rise and fall of the House of Labor, and the other one is tracking working-class New York as the protagonist. You describe the personality, the collective culture of New York’s working class, the way they lived life together, and the way it expresses itself in class conflict. In the strike wave that succeeded the Second World War, how was the militancy of the New York working class a reflection of general historical and economic conditions—what you call a non-Fordist economy in the age of Ford?

I'm not a big historiographically oriented fellow, but two things struck me. One was the story of post-World War Two New York, which back then was completely celebratory. It was Jackson Pollock and Broadway musicals and glitzy architecture. It was a success story, and the entire world of working people was just absent. So I wanted to fill that in and show how they helped shape the city.

The other is the historiography of labor. The generation of New Left historians that I was at the tail end of very much focused on the CIO and lamented what they saw as its deradicalization. That's where the story was. It's the rise and then eventual deradicalization of the CIO.

But New York City was an AFL town; it wasn't a town of big industry, like Detroit or Chicago. The “non-Fordist” formulation was to look for the economic underpinnings of this different kind of labor movement, featuring a different kind of work environment, which I think had not just political implications, but had cultural implications too. There's been some very interesting work since my book that looks at what unions are doing well now. They’re mostly old AFL unions; they're not the old CIO unions.

How long did it take you to write this?

10 years. Every book I've ever written until the last one, took 10 years. I had a job while writing.

A good working class historian should be working. I guess you grew up during the Cold War,. I wanted to ask how the Cold War was used as a tool of class war. Obviously there's Taft-Hartley in 1947, which undermined the labor movement. Truman almost used the National Guard against striking longshoremen in ‘46.

Look, anti-Communism and anti-radicalism have long histories in the United States, really long histories. Even before World War II in the late 30s, there was a big anti-Communist mobilization, which a lot of the scholars have argued was really aimed at more than just literally the Communist Party. It was aimed at a whole broader world of left-wing thinking and left-wing culture.

It's not inaccurate to say that there was a tremendous influence of the left on American life at the time, whether in Hollywood or the labor movement. But the conflation of all kinds of progressive efforts with Communism was a useful vehicle: companies trying to defeat a union claim to be going after a bunch of “reds,” and so on. But it goes deeper than that. There is a deep discomfort with a lot of things associated with the left, some of which are just things associated with modernity.

Gender and race, for example.

Exactly. And that counteroffensive starts in the late 1930s, but it's suspended during the war because of the American-Soviet Alliance, then breaks out very quickly again at the end of the war and is really one of the transformative forces in American life. In the second half of the 20th century, including in New York and in terms of institutions, it's pretty devastating. It destroys all kinds of mass organizations.

Now, I argue that a lot of that Popular Front left kind of manages to survive semi-underground in some cases by disassociating itself from the Communist Party, because its ideas were not just restricted to the far left. One of the things that really struck me is how the AFL, generally considered a conservative entity, was on certain matters, like social benefits for workers, even more advanced than some of the left-wing unions.

Really?

Yeah. Fighting for health insurance for union members, for example. So the damage was done by the anti-Communism of the Cold War, but left influence remains. It never completely disappears—though it becomes more subdued through coalitions and not proclaiming its broadest conceptions about its differences with mainstream liberalism.

Failing to transition from a class-in-itself to a class-for-itself, as Marx would say. Could you discuss the effects of the AFL-CIO merger?

They merged in 1955 in New York. The differences between the two by the mid-1950s weren’’t as strong as they used to be, in part because of the Cold War and the de-radicalization of much of the CIO. The CIO had lost a lot of momentum. The purge of the left was very costly, not just in terms of sheer numbers, but also in terms of an organizing impulse, the broader ambition about what was possible. There was also a lot of internal fighting inside the CIO. The merger solved a lot of internal problems.

I've generally associated the AFL with what Lenin once disparaged as mere “trade unionism.” But your book has made me reconsider my antipathies. If we appreciate the working-class character of New York, perhaps we should show the AFL a bit more love. But, on the other hand, you also suggest that the AFL introduces elements of the corporatism that’s eventually imposed on the working class from above in the fiscal crisis of the mid-70s. So there's a way in which they become complicit with that logic that eventually kneecaps them.

By the 70s and the fiscal crisis, I'm not sure there's much difference between unions. But within the AFL, they come up with mechanisms to assert workers' power to defend workers in specific economic contexts, often industries characterized by a lot of competition, by a lot of small employers, which is true of the garment industry, the construction industry, and some others. That requires a certain kind of flexibility on their part coming up with an organizational model, which I don't think is given enough credit for its effectiveness.

The district councils are important here. They're based on specific crafts, or specific employers, or sometimes specific ethnicities. In this model, you're building solidarity based on a sort of localist basis. Here, the real power of the union lies in the district council, which all these locals fold into, cutting across all manner of parochial boundaries. It's a model that comes out of the garment industry, but a lot of the construction industry uses it also, and eventually the AFSCME District Council 37. It was an effective way of organizing, because you don’t have these giant plants with 2,000 or 4,000 people, where the plant itself is creating this kind of solidarity that cuts across occupational and ethnic lines. In New York, people are working in places with 20 people.

I think these are some distinctive AFL things, which were very strong in New York and proved to be rather successful. And because a lot of these employers were small, it also meant things like benefits operated differently—who's responsible for figuring out how people get pensions, how they get healthcare and health insurance and so forth.

Now, if you were bargaining with US Steel or GM, they've got some vast HR department to handle such matters. If you were bargaining with some painting contractor—a guy and his brother-in-law and 7 workers—they have no clue about any of this. So the expertise actually develops in the union more than the employer. Even on things like efficient management, often the unions know a lot more than the employers do.

Would you say, then, this led to a kind of institutionalization of the unions in government? I’m thinking especially of the Robert Wagner mayoralty (1954-1965).

I read the minutes of the AFL and the CIO Central Labor Councils one summer. It was all on microfilm. It was a nightmare. But it was interesting how much the AFL dealt with government issues, in some ways more than the CIO, which you might think of as the more political of the two. The AFL often dealt with government, but on the very narrow grounds of what impacted their members. So you get things like the printing trades: they were big on how elections were run because they wanted to make sure that there were paper ballots coming from union printers. It was a job creation. They had an Albany lobbyist working on this.

Politicians like mayor Wagner were extremely deferential to organized labor, both in symbolic but also in real ways. So unions did become very intertwined with governance, but not necessarily promoting broad visionary ideas. It tends to be incrementalist and particularist.

How did this change by 1969? Your chapter “Long Hairs and Hard Hats” approaches the global ‘68 from the standpoint of New York City. CUNY was an inflection point in all of this, of course. But there's the question of broader politics, especially the imperial politics of America’s war in Vietnam—the “hardhats” representing flag-waving patriots, the “longhairs” representing young anti-war radicals.

By the late 60s, a million people in New York were in the labor movement, so it was hit by the same cultural and political divides that impacted the whole society.

There are elements of the labor movement that are very much part of that ‘68 impulse. There are a number of important unions that come out against the war of Vietnam, for example. A lot of the big liberal national unions support LBJ, and they support the war of Vietnam because they're anti-communist, and because they want to stay in favor with the Johnson administration: they think it's good for labor. But in New York, there were a number of unions that broke with that as early as 1965, and by 68, a big chunk of the local labor movement had followed suit. But obviously, there are a lot of other unions that are very strong and supportive of the war because they believe in it and are critical of some of the New Left elements that are coming up.

Globally, 1968 is an extraordinary moment of challenge to the established sets of relations that grew out of World War II, but mostly it's defeated. Mostly it's rolled back. In New York, that contest is pretty intense.

This also aligns with the CUNY open admissions fight in 1969.

The CUNY story is really fascinating and complicated. It's hard to summarize quickly. There were a couple things about CUNY I didn't completely understand when I wrote the book. One was that we always followed the narrative that, at first CUNY was free, but it was hard to get into. Then there was open admissions, and then they imposed tuition. But it turned out that if you go back to the 1950s, only half of CUNY was free. It was only free for full-time day students.

It’d got increasingly difficult to get into CUNY colleges. You needed a good high school grade average to get into colleges like Queens or Brooklyn or City College. So a lot of kids would go at night, for which admission standards were lower and also they could work—that was not free of charge. And they were the more working class students. So we tend to have this narrative that the story is free tuition, then open admissions, then tuition, but actually the real narrative is half free, half pay, then a hugely chaotic middle period, and today, we're back to half free and half pay, because if you look at TAP and all that, half of CUNY students don't pay tuition. So it's actually not that different than it was seventy years ago.

The open admissions issue was that it was increasingly difficult to get into CUNY schools. Many families, especially Black families, felt that their kids were being kept from having the opportunities that other New Yorkers were getting. They were paying taxes like everybody else to support these schools. There was a growing sense that the process was discriminatory—which in many ways it was. But the odd thing about it, which I don’t think was fully publicized, but I think the labor people understood, was that it wasn't just non-whites who were being shut out. There were a lot of working class whites who also couldn't get into CUNY. So labor supported open enrollment. They didn't support affirmative action—they supported open enrollment, which are really different things. The original protestors at City College, if I understand correctly, were really more for affirmative action. They wanted the student body at City College to reflect the makeup of the population in that part of the city. That's a kind of equity and opportunity demand. The outcome of that struggle was not what they were asking for, but it was open enrollment, which threw open the doors to everybody. And the biggest increase in CUNY enrollment, if you break it down by ethnicity and nationality, was among Italian-Americans.

That was one of the more unexpected facts in the book.

The mainstream labor leaders were savvy about this stuff, they were all for it because their members' kids weren't getting into CUNY. Now, of course, this created a big backlash. It was seen as pandering by a lot of people, and it justified an anti-Civil Rights backlash. Also, it created tremendous logistical problems with capacity issues. It’s more or less the kind of stuff the city's facing right now for New York’s Universal childcare program. If you throw open the doors to everybody to get free childcare from six months up, how do you do it? Well, that's what CUNY faced, and it didn't always do a great job, and that was a reputational hit. So it was a complicated period.

Then it also led almost immediately into the big downturn of ‘73.

Yes. These happened in very rapid succession. The economic crisis of the western world that happened in the early 1970s had a huge impact on city government, city budgets. And it became the opportunity for a reactionary mobilization that in New York got crystallized by the fiscal crisis. As a result of changes in the regional economy, the deindustrialization of the city, the outflow of residents, particularly white population decline, the tax base was shrinking while simultaneously the conception of what government should be was expanding. And then the economy fell apart.

In the short term the city borrowed to cover the gap, egged on by the banks who make a lot of money doing this. But you can't really have “social democracy in one city.” The legitimating functions of the state, those that maintained loyalty, were becoming increasingly expensive. It was becoming hard to finance.

The city couldn’t sell bonds anymore. This became the opportunity for a conservative movement among intellectuals, but also in the finance industry, which had been almost sidelined in social democratic New York. I mean, it still ran banks and other institutions, but in terms of setting the tenor of society and politics, not so much. Conservatives and financiers had witnessed social values shifting in ways that they found deeply disturbing. And this was the great opportunity to launch their ideological, fiscal and political counter-revolution.

It was a coup in some ways. They set up a sort of fiscal Vichy government.

That's a very good way of thinking about it. Not that long ago Kim Phillips Fein, wrote a terrific book, Fear City, that details this revanche. She shows this moment as not just originating in the local finance community in New York—it's also coming out of the Ford administration, a real concerted effort coming out of Washington to promote this kind of a program.

But William E. Simon, the Secretary of Treasury under Gerald Ford, was a New Yorker, right?

Yeah. He was a New Yorker. He was a bond salesman. The whole history of municipal bonds and municipal funds is completely fascinating. There are moments when it's a very profitable industry, but it can be perilous because cities go kaput. So the fiscal crisis is the pivot of the book. I argue that it marks the end of the advances of this whole post-war world of working class New York—its institutional structures; the labor movement; but also liberal third parties and tenants groups; and a whole array of political organizations. They're stopped in their tracks in ‘75 and pushed back. And there were obvious kinds of takebacks that affected the standard of living of ordinary people: raising the subway fare, putting tuition in at CUNY, etc.

But it's not as if all advances were completely eradicated. I mean, here we are in New York City, and we still have rent control on a million apartments, and conservatives are still going bananas. Atlanta bulldozed every public housing. You can't knock down a single unit of public housing in some of the fanciest neighbors in New York. To me, that's a measure of how much this world was not eradicated.

You do get the impression that once neighborhoods distinctly existed, reading your book or talking to older New Yorkers. Maybe they still do exist, but the prevalence of neighborhoods in the cityscape has absolutely diminished over time.

Yes. It's diminished. It's not disappeared, but it's diminished. For example, a lot of New York City playgrounds before the fiscal crisis, they'd be staffed and they'd be a recreation guy or usually a guy who'd be a kind of parental figure. He's the guy you go to when you need the basketball, but he kind of keep an eye on kids. He'd be organizing programs. Most of that's gone. So people turn elsewhere. In the preface to the new edition of the book, I assert that ethnicity in some ways is more important than ever in New York, in part because ethnic bonds fill the gap that's left by the retreat of the state. So ethnic associations, just like they did a hundred years ago, are the place you turn when your family's in trouble. It's a highly organized world in which there are business associations and youth groups and language schools. These are the places that you turn to for help, for mutual support, for cultural enrichment, for youth activities.

Maybe there's also just a difference in demographic flows or the way in which integration happens in the city.

If there are three demographic blocks that are the core of my book, it's the children of white immigrants, African-Americans and Puerto Ricans. The 1965 Immigration Reform Act changes all that. We are now at levels of the percentage of the city that's foreign born that are approaching the historic highs of the early 20th century. We are a much more immigrant city today than the immediate post-World War II.

Compared to maybe 40-50 years ago, we’re more like the New York of 120 years ago where you have a kind of elite, a ruling sector that is deeply unaware of what most of the city is like. You're going back all the way back to Jacob Riis, “how the other half lives.” To me, the great tip off was in the Democratic primary debate for mayor, when Mamdani asked Andrew Cuomo which mosques he visited while he held the office. And Cuomo couldn't name one. He had never visited a mosque. He was the governor of New York for 10 years. It's extraordinary.

It's a testament to the provincialism that afflicts the upper class in New York. To round out in the present, what do you see as the fundamental shift in the 21st century from as Working-Class New York is reissued? We have a socialist mayor—if you were to give him this book, which chapter would you tell him to read?

If I gave him this book, I'd say, would you write a blurb? [Laughter.]

It is very hard to synthesize everything that's changed in New York. Clearly there's greater inequality, even greater inequality than 25 years ago. Another is the ever greater power of the interlocked finance and real estate industries. Sam Stein, who's a terrific scholar, who got his Ph.D. at the Graduate Center wrote a book about NYC in which he coined the term “real estate state.” Even under progressives like de Blasio, the real estate industry had quite a bit of sway. So we will see how they respond to Zohran’s mayoralty; the story isn’t yet written.

And then of course the tremendous increase in the foreign-born population that has certainly transformed the fabric and everyday life of New York. In many ways, enriching it enormously. It's quite extraordinary, from cuisine to arts to so many other things. It's a different world.

There is also the growth of a large precarious, professional middle class in tech fields, education, cultural industries, social services, health services, people who in some ways are doing pretty well, but feel very uncertain about their own future.

They can't really own very much.

Yeah, exactly. Very disillusioned with what they expected. They are one component of the base that brought the mayor to power, along with Muslims, south Asians, young voters. On one hand they're the gentrifier. On the other hand, they have three roommates on the floor of the building that they gentrified. They can't afford to live there. So they have three roommates and they're wondering why they got that degree. So that's another big change in New York.

It is a very fluid moment. It could go lots of different ways. I mean, the economy is what it is and the mayor has very limited influence on it, but who governs and how they govern does make a big difference. This is an unusual experiment that we've launched on. So we'll see what happens.

The word “take” has many resonances in the English language and one of them is to capture by violence. This meaning survives most commonly in chess and parts of news media that cover global geopolitics. To take is to dispossess, to strip bare, to occupy, and perhaps, to steal. An associated meaning is to stabilize something ephemeral by recording it: taking a photograph, taking notes, taking as écriture, as the literalization of a fleeting target before it disappears. A third, passive sense moves in the opposite direction and points at a loss of control, a fraying consciousness, an unraveling force in face of an exalted encounter: “I was quite taken by the Seurats.”

John Strasbaugh’s recent semi-biography of Marcel Duchamp, out in time to coincide with the MoMA retrospective, takes on these differing yet complimentary senses with a specific focus on the artist’s life, narrowed down to his time in New York City. Opting against the more conventional biographical line, Strasbaugh offers in this slim, but satisfactory volume a fragmented and concise summary of how Duchamp conquered New York, photographed, and catalogued it, and how New York, in turn, was taken by his “an-artistic” provocations, unlike anywhere else in the world. Duchamp, as is well-documented, was virtually unknown in his native France during his lifetime, never had a solo exhibition there, and was assumed to be a lesser artist than his sculptor brother Raymond Duchamp-Villon. The twenty or so years Duchamp spent in France when New York fell under the law of Prohibition are omitted here, as are his spells in Munich and Buenos Aires, and his life as an impoverished Manhattanite is prioritized instead. Told mostly through Duchamp’s social relationships—Man Ray and Beatrice Wood at one end of the spectrum, Peggy Guggenheim and Andy Warhol on the other—Marcel Duchamp Takes New York localizes the artist in the modernist circles of the new world and diligently maps out his oeuvre across the recognizable landscapes of the city, retracing his steps in the wires and dust of the Upper West Side, the Village, Hale House, and numerous downtown studios.

A historian of Greenwich village and recreational drug use, Strasbaugh plays to his strengths as a chronicler of downtown bohos and offers a salutary take on Duchamp that treats the artist as a larger-than-life rulebreaker who never had a shortage of interesting bon-mots, and whose every act bore the irremovable trace of legend. Captured by the artist through careful calculation, and a bit of luck, New York emerges in this narrative as the capital of the twentieth century, the machinic future city of cars, ferries, and tall buildings that is etched into one’s memory in the brooding images of Alfred Stieglitz. While this industrial metropole was certainly the right place for Duchamp, it was almost the wrong time. Unable to adapt its art and sensibility to the demands of the present, New York was ruled by cultural conservatism, represented in this book by the “lamentable arch” (to quote Henry James) in Washington Square with its comically neo-classical statue of the first president. Despite this conservative attitude in visual art, the United States did not have an overbearing history, an “indestructible traditionalism” like France and England did, which Duchamp found liberating. His work and personality were equally transformed by the American touch. His shy Norman outlook was shed in favour of a more ironic self-expression, and his art increasingly turned self-referential and humorous. The Americans were not “grandsons of Hugo or Shakespeare,” they did not act like the descendants of some great men. The lack of burdensome history made New York a laboratory for modernist invention, “a perfect terrain for new developments.”

Duchamp’s quasi-futurist nude descended onto the 1913 Armory Show as the artist rested at his Neuilly home, unaware that he had become an overnight celebrity in North America, a reputation “equalled only by Napoleon and Sarah Bernhardt,” according to his friend Henri-Pierre Roché. The painting had little luck in Europe prior, as the Cubists were reluctant to embrace it and refused to show it at the 1912 Salon des Independentes. Although Appolinaire’s book on Cubist painters would later include Duchamp in a short, valedictory chapter, this refusal arguably colored Duchamp’s complicated stance towards the avant-garde movements of his time. His work shared some undeniable elements from Cubism, Dada, and Futurism, but he often distanced himself from being associated with any of them directly. To be part of a movement meant being recognizable, and being recognizable was the sign that one was repeating oneself. It was Duchamp’s decision to inscribe the title of the work into the painting alienated and angered many European modernists, who despite their visual inventiveness were still wedded to a belief in the autonomous artwork and held to a firm distinction between what the eye saw and what the mind recorded. Duchamp’s Nude, while not entirely there yet, registered a premonitory wish to collapse the difference between the two. It presented a static visual experience, created by the hand with a tube of paint, but of constant movement by depicting an androgynous subject whose action was caught in the perpetual growth of time. By introducing a temporal dimension into the space of art, Duchamp’s work cultivated a resistance to visual interpretation and engendered an imaginative gridlock in the viewer, a retinal impasse that allowed them to interrogate the primacy of seeing, to displace judgements of beauty and ugliness, and shift the questions more in the direction of art and non-art.

Duchamp’s biographer Calvin Tomkins maintained that it was Matisse’s The Blue Nude that truly upset The Armory Show, greeted as “epileptic,” “coarse,” and “depraved,” while Duchamp’s Nude received a more ambivalent reception. It drew large crowds, inspired some parodies in the local newspapers, like the famous “The Rude Descending the Staircase,” and remained for the most part the subject of humor rather than aesthetic derision, even though Teddy Roosevelt had famously commented in Outlook Magazine that his Navajo rug was a better work of art than Duchamp’s temporally squeezed nude, an accidentally Primitivist take by the scourge of the Philippines.

Following this account closely, Strausbaugh preserves the monumental myth of the Armory Show as the hinge point at which modern art invaded the American sensibility, turning “landscape painters into Cubist painters the next morning.” Such paradigm shifts are of course difficult to pin-down with precision as historical change, like the figure in Duchamp’s painting, is always over-determined by an irreducible variety of forces and does not yield easily to conceptual constructs. Yet the significance of the Nude, as the zero degree of Duchampian transgression, is impossible to overcome. “The scandal was exactly in my program,” Duchamp was to reflect in his later years on Nude, thoroughly content with the unexpected afterlife the painting had. While scandal often forms the focal point of Nude-interpretations, the key word in his remark should be “program.” For that word is an admission on Duchamp’s part that, contrary to the European avant-gardes of his time, the spontaneous force of sensation had for him little purchase, and the thought-process involved in the making and canonisation of art was the real pay-off. The scandal was the program; the great sin of the painting was that it no longer sought to please the demands of the eye, nor satisfy the mastery of the hand, but wished to escape the ever-expanding fortress of physicality in order to put painting “in service of the mind.”

The most intriguing part of Strasbaugh’s book is certainly the origins of Duchamp’s most famous succès de scandale, Fountain. Was it truly Duchamp who conceived of this readymade and submitted it to the Society of Independent Artists show (modeled on the Parisian one) in order to challenge and upset his friends whose ideas on art he deemed too narrow-minded? Or was it the amateur readymade artist Baroness Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven who submitted the work under the pseudonym “R. Mutt” (as Duchamp seems to indicate in one letter to his sister when he mentions the involvement of a “female friend”)? Proponents of the Baroness theory intimate that it was indeed she who bought the urinal from a hardware store in Philadelphia and it was only after her death that Duchamp began to claim authorship of the work with his boîte-en-valise.

Strasbaugh gives us both stories, both “takes” to let the reader decide. It deserves mentioning, however, that the so-called “Baroness authorship theory” (incidentally Walter Arsenberg, one of Duchamp’s friends and a key figure in the SIA show, had a lifelong obsession with the similarly intractable Shakespeare-Francis Bacon debate) was in part devised as a counter-origin story with the purpose of discrediting modern art en masse.
