Plainly articulated in Glyn Thompson’s 2014 study Duchamp’s Urinal: The Facts Behind the Facade, an aggrieved pro-Elsa book notable for its freewheeling approach, the Baroness theory is a thinly-veiled attempt to recast Duchamp as a masquerading art-thief, to discredit Conceptual Art as a hoax, and to reinstate reactionary categories like intentionality and authorship to art history. Numerous articles have been devoted by scholars like Dawn Ades and Bradley Bailey to debunking the Baroness-theory in recent years, and their arguments with Thompson, sadistically entertaining in their own right, do not need repeating here. Yet this virulent debate remains significant as it threads several modernist faultlines. For it is not simply the case that followers of the Baroness misattribute the origins of the artwork, and are unable to correct their mistakes by looking at the relevant evidence in the Duchamp archives. Rather the way they approach Fountain displays a fundamental misunderstanding about how art works, a misunderstanding that is so widespread and residual that its anti-intellectual, anti-aesthetic, and anti-modernist sentiment often passes unnoticed. Since the work itself was programmed to destabilize the signature of the artist, such headfirst dives into the authorship debate is inevitably at odds with the spirit of Fountain. Unwilling to judge modernism on its own terms, the Fountain authorship debate risks restoring outdated concepts like originary creation back to aesthetic criticism and threatens to impose an obsolete art historical model on the readymade, a model from which it desperately wanted to declare its independence.

Either way, the fact remains that Fountain is seen and debated a century later with more or less the same kind of confusion, anger, and inquiry that it generated in the first place. Its displacement of signature and never-ending capacity to shock endures, along with its unusual power—a power that comes from having resigned all the traditional capacities of art in search of something more effective. Not exhibited in 1917, Fountain made waves when Stieglitz’s famous photograph of the readymade was published in the Dada journal The Blind Man. The decision not to exhibit the work was already controversial, since SIA followed a “no jury, no prizes” ethos and everyone who paid the six dollar fee and submitted their work on time counted as an artist. Angered by the refusal to exhibit Fountain, Duchamp’s friend, and the future partner of Edgar Varese, Louise Norton penned an article in The Blind Man that compared SIA to the philosophers in Dante’s hell, those backward-looking ghosts whose heads were placed the wrong way on their shoulders. “I suppose monkeys hated losing their tails,” Norton wrote, “there is death in every change, and we monkeys do not like death as we should.”

For a brief moment Richard Mutt was the talk of the town, but as we monkeys do not like to evolve, his telegram arrived with a fifty year delay (a fitting gap for the master of time dilation) becoming the ancestor of “anything goes” in that period of utmost crisis in Western self-confidence, the 1970s. In his recent study Duchamp’s Telegram, Thierry de Duve suggested that Fountain marked the rapturous turning point in Western aesthetics from beaux-arts to “arts-in-general” (de Duve’s term for our current aesthetic model where “anything whatsoever” can be art), transforming the age-old “is it beautiful?” question into the devilish “is it art?”—a schema that both builds on his earlier work, like Kant After Duchamp, and echoes Jacques Ranciere’s work on the aesthetic regime of art with its emphasis on the potential of the ordinary to enter the previously guarded domains of aesthetic experience. Regarding our preference for the aesthetic regime of art or arts-in-general, the turning point might move forward or backward, but Fountain undoubtedly deserves its place in the world-historical tsunami that swept over the globe in 1917—the year that was etched below the pseudonym on the urinal, and marked one of the deadliest years of the Great War. That year the Bolsheviks stormed the Winter Palace, the British signed the Balfour Declaration and split Palestine, the first jazz record was released, and Duchamp telegrammed Fountain. One can argue endlessly if it was indeed Fountain that singularly crossed the threshold of representation, or if it simply marked the moment where after a long period of nutrition a sense of change became irrefutable. 1917 witnessed that spirit of change break with the world, and we continue to inhabit the divided sphere where Fountain and the readymade remain our untimely contemporaries, bearers of the bygone flash that can show us what the new looks like.

While Strasbaugh’s story conveniently places the readymades at the center of Duchamp’s American invasion, it perhaps underemphasizes how often Duchamp’s move towards the cosa mentale was interlinked with repeated insinuations of sex and the body. We are reminded of his "legendary sex life,” but the sexual mise-en-scene of his works, always winking behind the conceptual edifice, elicits minimal attention. Duchamp’s works often invite us to partake in an aesthetic experience that goes beyond the sensations of the visible, to approach art as a mental exercise that allows access to an invisible plane, to an ulterior, temporal dimension. Yet simultaneously evoked are licentious innuendos addressed powerfully to the eye. Think of the vulgar simplicity of L.H.O.O.Q., the gender outlaw Rrose Selavy, the complex scientia sexualis behind The “Large” Glass (with its love gasoline and chocolate grinder) or the notorious spread-eagle that awaits behind the peep-hole in Étants Donnés. The readymade, may stage a physical confrontation for a type of struggle that primarily takes place in the mind, but so many of Duchamp’s great works resort to corporeal elements that complicate the conceptual purity of his intentions. Perhaps to undercut their seriousness with a dose of irreverent play, or to underline how thought can never be separated from the body, these works serve as a reminder that one cannot solely exist, as Descartes hoped to, like a brain in a jar. To see, to think, to be a body in space and time is a paradoxical experience whose frustrations art certainly cannot alleviate but can turn into aporetic questions. Art is never the solution for Duchamp, but a game that collapses on itself the moment it is begun to be played. It is a game that we are invited to take part in, but one that requires us to radically leave behind our conceptions about what a game might even be, one that forces us to rethink the changing rules at each turn, and leaves us in the end with little more than the fragility of our ideas and the uncanniness of our sense. The rules of the game are decided upon each time by the participants and should they wish to alter them, as the readymades often demand, they must be willing to take a leap into the realm of the unexpected and reposition themselves in face of radical uncertainty. “No course of action could be determined by a rule,” Wittgenstein famously wrote, “because any course of action can be made out to accord with the rule.” The readymade thus emerges in Strasbaugh’s narrative as the key victory in the Duchampian conquest of rules. It is the shock of the readymade that will deliver the left-behind American art into its formidable next stage, a stage where the dramas of artistic activity will no longer follow the same procedures and codes that allowed it to be expressed hitherto. No different than a pawn, on the chessboard-like grid, New York will be taken by Duchamp, dispossessed of its decorations, its actors, its voice, and its taste, leaving behind only the beauty of indifference.

A take is always a take-over; and Duchamp was well-aware of the conceptual violence his artworks were causing in their displays. Taste and “retinal art” had to be destroyed to allow for the birth of something new, and only through capturing New York could the new be facilitated and energized. While never his direct subject per se, Strausbaugh’s book implies through limiting its focus on Duchamp’s art to his excursions in the city that it is always New York that is recorded in his art. New York as the embodiment of a modernist spirit, as the unification of man and machine, as the emblem of a willingness to playfully rebel. Yet in the postwar years, Duchamp was not the sole heir to the crown, as he undoubtedly stood at odds with the other modernists of the city, namely Abstract Expressionism. Mutually hostile to one another, Duchamp viewed Ab-Ex as the return of retinalism he intensely sought to undermine in the earlier part of the century. Instead of ideas, puns, and signifiers, strong feelings and expressions were restored to art, erecting the kingdom of the eye once more. Duchamp’s dislike of Ab-Ex was such that he suggested to Peggy Guggenheim that she cut out the edges of a Pollock to fit it into a room, since “nobody would notice the difference,” implying that the overflowing states of inner experience Ab-Ex excelled at lacked the kind of precision he sought in an artwork.

As modernism was theorized in the postwar years by Clement Greenberg as a movement towards flatness and medium-specificity, Duchamp was vilified as an “avant-gardist” who himself was not avant-garde, a Futurist radical whose works did not aspire to the required conditions of formal breakthrough and whose art failed to will “the unknown” into being. Repositioned as the originator of post-modernism, Duchamp found himself reduced in postwar New York to an artist who resorted to “ingenuity instead of inspiration, contrivance instead of creation.” To win, however, sometimes one has to sacrifice some pieces, fall back, and rearrange the scene, and Duchamp’s temporary defeat at the hands of Greenberg and Ab-Ex (with the notable exception of Motherwell, whose book on Dada played a significant role in the transmission of his legacy) can perhaps be better understood as a prelude to his eventual reclamation by Pop and Conceptual Art, a momentary retreat that repositioned “Dada’s Daddy” as the accursed progenitor of “art as idea.”

One take-away from Strasbaugh’s book is the psychological need to think of artists in terms of locations and to place them upon a geographical scale. Chasing links between the artists we love and the cities we inhabit is an intellectual plaything whose seductive charms are difficult to resist; we engage in this game to make our lives feel more expansive and consequential, to awaken our regulated rhythms of quotidian toil to the possibility of historical greatness. We say to New York: “Duchamp needs you. Warhol needs you. Cage needs you.” But in our attempts to alert such dignitaries of how indispensable the city had been to the creation of their singular accents, we often overlook the fact that their need for these cities pales greatly in comparison to the intensity with which we need them—since it is we who ask them to play Virgil to our urban self-actualization and reanimate their bygone spirits at each crossroads, we who have resurrected their memory and repurposed it to fit our momentary desires, we who have violently ripped their phrases from their resting place and demanded they perform a perpetual danse macabre for the satisfaction of our low and uncreative times. Indeed, we must repeat this ritual with gruesome blindness, because how otherwise can a fleeting meaning be restored to avenues, streets, and apartments, names be etched across the walls, and the signature of the artist once again roam freely over the anonymous mass? But the ghost of Duchamp can no more tell us about New York than the disembodied spirits who are summoned by a medium from the land of the dead can tell us about the experience of dying. What comes out of Marcel Duchamp Takes New York is in the end a kind of split, a resignation, and a disavowal; an implication that to take New York is to be taken in return, and that only those capable of sacrificing their strong self-attachments and eager to display their internal division are likely to succeed in such an act, a success that might have more in common with failure than initially assumed. The enigma of Duchamp persists in no small part due to his ability to exhibit that split with utmost willingness, to perceive himself and his work as the work of another, and to indulge in that strangeness so many artists are afraid of, one that perennially confronts the viewer in a spiral and whirls toward the edges of the unthinkable.

By Theadora Williams

It’s not too much to say that we live in “interesting times,” and among the more unwelcome recent developments has been whispers of a new “Lavender Scare.” As many parallels as we can draw between them, we must look at historical genocides and the way they targeted trans people to properly understand the present moment

The original “Lavender Scare” (a term popularized by David K. Johnson’s eponymous book, The Lavender Scare: The Cold War Persecution of Gays and Lesbians in the Federal Government) ran parallel to McCarthy’s purges of communists and included both the moral panic about the presence of gays in government and their subsequent purges. The Red and Lavender Scares were intrinsically linked—-“subversives” in media and political speeches could mean communists and homosexuals alike. To oppose his crusade, McCarthy said, “you’ve got to be either a Communist or a cocksucker.” While the main anti-communist purges of McCarthy ended in the mid-1950s, the anti-gay purges persisted for far longer.

Between the late 1940s and early 1950s, State Department memos on the “Problem of Homosexuals and Sex Perverts in the Department of State“ were published, arguing that homosexuality led to civilizational decline; this was paired with the establishment of a Senate subcommittee tasked with investigating “Employment of Homosexuals and Other Sex Perverts in Government.” The committee, which received bipartisan support, concluded homosexuals were blackmailable, presented a security risk and were thus unsuitable for federal employment.

The zenith of this scare was President Eisenhower’s Executive Order 10450 (1953). It directed the federal government to investigate security risks including “sexual perversion” and led to the firings of over 5,000 federal employees. At the same time, the medical establishment further codified its own discrimination against homosexuals in textbooks and reference manuals. The American Psychological Association’s (APA) Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), first published in 1952, cast homosexuality as a “sociopathic personality disturbance.”

The effects of the scare lasted decades. It wasn’t until 1973 that the APA voted to remove “homosexuality” as a disorder entirely. The same year, a federal judge ruled that sexuality couldn’t be the sole factor in termination from federal employment. But further progress was slow. In 1995, President Clinton rescinded the order in place of the “Don’t Ask Don’t Tell” policy. But it was only in 2017 that President Obama explicitly revoked it.

There are plenty of parallels in today’s politics—one needs only look at government officials and far-right pundits fearmongering about “Trantifa” and “far-left gender ideology”; election-year ads proclaiming that “Kamala is for they/them, Trump is for you”; and more importantly, the purges of LGBTQ people from the federal government. So what is different this time around? The scale.

On Trump’s first day in office he signed Executive Order 14168, mandating that the federal government cease to recognize the existence of transgender people. Stipulated among the Order: no promotion or funding of “gender ideology,” no gender changes on passports, exclusion of trans people from all federal bathrooms, no trans healthcare for prisoners, and an attempt to repeal Bostock v. Clayton County, which found discrimination due to sexual orientation or gender identity to be discrimination on the basis of sex. The mandate purges the term “transgender” from as many places as possible, sometimes getting rid of the offending document whole-cloth. L’

That was the first executive order. Number 14183 barred trans people from the military and 14187 cut all federal funding for trans youth’s healthcare for those under 19 (perhaps to include 18 year olds precisely to target universities). 14190 directed law enforcement to criminally prosecute anybody who uses a trans child’s chosen name or pronouns in K-12 schools; moreover, to charge them with practicing medicine without a license and committing sexual exploitation of a minor. Read that again: Charging people with sex crimes for using a child’s chosen name.

Even the Lavender Scare did not resort to such tactics, largely because it didn’t entail a rollback of existing legal protections or culture of tolerance. It didn’t include these attacks on documents and travel, attacks on healthcare, and attacks on institutions of knowledge, for the simple reason these protections didn’t exist. While there are clear resonances between the two eras, we must compare another historical transition to understand this blitz on the trans community. Regrettably, we have one: the Nazi takeover of Weimar Germany and attacks on the first homosexual liberation movement.

In Berlin at the turn of the century, the Institute for Sexology pioneered early trans healthcare. Created by Magnus Hirschfeld, a gay Jewish doctor who ran the world’s first gay rights organization, the Institute pushed to establish “transvestite passes” and passports, which allowed trans people to dress as they wished. The media positively discussed trans people and advancements in healthcare and scientific understanding, often interviewing Hirschfeld. The Institute for Sexology was the world’s largest research library on all aspects of sex and sexuality in humans.

It was also the first target of the Nazi book burning, at which Goebbels addressed a crowd of 40,000. It was the first step in what Matt Fuller and Leah Owen 2022 refer to as a memoricide: the willful destruction of the memories and cultural treasures of an adversary – of queer people in Nazi Germany. The passes were, needless to say, revoked.

But even leading up to that, Nazi politicians would frequently rail against the dangers of homosexuality to the state and decry it as a Jewish plot. Homosexuality, in their terms, was “contagious.” Persecution of homosexuals became, following the Night of Long Knives, a priority of the Nazi police apparatus. But it was only until 1935 that homosexuals began to be placed in concentration camps, previously just being placed in the prisons. In both, they died and were killed at higher rates than peers, worked to death and often subjected to medical experimentation to “cure” them.

The anti-trans moral panic of the 21st century has many parallels with the McCarthyite Lavender Scare — the association of LGBT people with the left and destruction of civilization and the exclusion of LGBT people from the federal government. But that also applies to the Nazi genocide. Using state power to attack LGBT people in any situation generally entails an internal purge, and identification of LGBT people with political enemies.

Two distinguishing factors unite the current panic with the Nazi attacks while setting it apart from the Lavender Scare — the rollback of existing rights and the associated memoricide.

The Nazis rose to power in a time of great advances in LGBT rights and organizing, of gay rights groups, research to improve trans healthcare, and even state recognition of trans identities. The Lavender Scare was, conversely, a crackdown on a group with no historical protection or codified rights. Similarly, the Nazis successfully sought to prevent and destroy research on LGBT people; this included a memoricide against trans people. The Lavender Scare likewise did not entail this, it did not attack research programs on homosexuality, or cut funding for it, or otherwise actively use state power to curtail medicine and science.

We are not only faced with rollbacks on trans rights and rights to freely move in public, but attacks on trans research funding, healthcare, and even mentions of the word “transgender”. Sexual misconduct charges for a teacher acknowledging a child’s identity. Sexual misconduct charges for trans people being in public and seen by children. A living memoricide and invisibilization of a people who were previously recognized and somewhat protected.

One further factor could unite them, but is still in flux, the targeting of trans civilians. There is a distinction between purging from the state apparatus and from the public itself. The Nazis charged queer people with the crime of their identity and sentenced them to prisons and extralegal concentration camps. Meanwhile, ICE has stopped counting detained trans people and removed all requirements for ICE camps to grant transgender detainees their healthcare or secure housing. ICE has detained trans travelers to the US and European countries have given travel advisories warning trans people against coming here. And the Heritage Foundation, whose project 2025 laid out the anti-trans blueprint Trump has followed, called for the FBI to treat “Transgender Ideology-Inspired Violent Extremism” (TIVE) as a new domestic terror threat, characterized by considering anti-trans rhetoric and policies “a form of violence.” As one can call for the eradication” of “transgenderism” at a CPAC conference or the state department can call for the disarming of all trans people, calling these what they are is “extremism.”

If we want to look even further back, we can see parallels to the European colonization of the Americas. While the genocide of indigenous peoples is well known, lesser known are the attacks on queer acceptance and people. Diverse genders and sexualities that were broadly respected by native peoples were explicitly attacked. Colonization was rhetorically justified through open disgust of native acceptance of queerness and claims of inferiority and barbarity tied to them. Sometimes the brutality was tying people to the mouth of cannons and firing, such as Tibira do Maranhão, sometimes it was rounding up queer indigenous people to feed them to dogs. Our modern bathroom bans have their precedent in the sex segregation imposed by colonizers, the public shaming and misgendering of trans students caught by missionaries. Smithers 2022 provided a deeply researched overview of these atrocities against the two-spirits, though it centered the European atrocities over the indigenous lives themselves. While it is not quite so similar, settler-colonialism and fascism, representing external and internal state repression respectively, the founding violence of this state bears thinking of. After all, fascism is colonialism turned inward, the “terrific boomerang” noted by Césaire.

Much like with the Nazis, or the colonizers of the Americas — trans people are not the chief target. As the Nazis attacked Jews first and foremost so has the US has attacked Hispanic people first and foremost and so the colonizers attacked indigeneity as a whole. The dehumanization, state repression, and denaturalization of citizens of this empire is best evidenced in extralegal death camps like CECOT. But in all we are a target. And unlike the Nazis, in much more explicit terms and with a greater focus.

My undergraduate sociology thesis, written in 2023, was a comparative historical analysis of trans organizing, rights, and healthcare in the United States, pre-colonization to present, and in Germany from Weimar to the Nazis. It bleakly predicted most of this. At the time, I rang the alarm bell loudly on the coalition of anti-trans groups like Genspect and the Society for Evidence Based Gender Medicine, the anti-trans strategies and rhetoric being increasingly adopted by the far-right, and their openly genocidal intent. And now here we are again.

With no understatement, the clear intent of the far-right for the past few years has been a genocide of the trans community. And we are witnessing nothing less than its opening stages. In these times, our only hope is a popular front, a rainbow coalition of the militant left, uniting to oppose the disappearance and targeting and repression of all targets of the state. The day I wrote this, Assata Shakur died, free from the clutches of the empire after a lifetime opposing it. Her words give me hope in these times, as I hope they may for you: “It is our duty to fight for our freedom. It is our duty to win.”

Lulu. Do we have to go out tonight? My nerves are bad and I am uncertain. I see a hundred flowers but not one that I can touch. I drift into dullness and mourn the horror of growing old. The morning of life was the best in its juvenile purity. The dampness of furs, the scent of rain-soaked leaves. The eerie fragrance of childhood scenes. The sun flooded us with intervals. Seduced by flowers, corals and the shimmer of shells. I talked to cousin Margaret among the colored-fish. The water was cold like a jewel. Papa said, Augusta, come, warm beside the fire. At night I listened the fireplace crack to the beat of a perishing moon. The birds charmed me at daybreak. I guess, we are going to that party after all. Odious and engulfed with absurdity, these nouveau riche. No taste left in gowns or lingerie. But the one marrying, to that dismal Schön, was you. Your white dress and razor black hair condemned the night, inadequate. I stammered and bit my lip. How did I keep my act serene? We tangoed to the incantation of an inner pull. A wave swept over my head. My hair set free, our eyes met. You can’t put a butterfly in a jar. Then there was the trial. On the run for mariticide. I asked about you meanwhile. No one spared, the stubborn opined: you were the ruin of all love. In your permeating fugitive gleam, you are the only one who can save me, you said. I did not have the courage to reply: “let’s forever leave this town.” I handed the passport and said: you play the Countess for a while. After sickness, care, and defeat. I mourn the last thing to come out of the box. As your sight and the century collapse into an echo.

 

Murder. SIR – We have all witnessed in recent years the resurgence of that stupendous claim on the pages of this very magazine, first voiced in an article by Mr. R. P. Daggers titled “MURDER – is it art?” Mr. Daggers insists, nay, provokes the readers of this fine magazine to contemplate a tempting and ludicrous proposal scorched in the lowliest confines of the human mind. By Jove, inferno has no terror for him. It is my wish here, sir, to intrude, and to reverse the salience of this claim now well-known and well-discussed in every coffeehouse in London. For it only takes a child’s knowledge to prove Mr. Daggers’ lewdsuggestions wrong and to demonstrate with Logic how the opposite is closer to the truth. I am positive that murder is not an art, as these murder-fanciers like Mr. Daggers have it, but art is a kind of murder. When an artist of esteemed character engages in an act dissecting the vicissitudes and the harshness of the times he finds he is handed a demonic power. A power, sir, from the most deep pits of hell that knows no limits other than its own which appears to every artist as instinct and a mystery. The great Shakespeare knew it well – as did his coterie of famed murderers, Macbeth and Caesar, Hamlet and Anthony, Othello and Richard. So did Milton, Pope, Swift, Gray, Warsh, King, Hammond, Gay, Rowe, Young, Mallet, Broome, Garth, Morel, Parnell and Akenside. With this sultry power the artist grants himself a charter to favor the embellishments of art over the pangs of life. The finest portrait painter of our age, Mr. Gainsborough, takes a soul each time he puts his hands on that sublime canvas of his. Who remembers these men and women that feature in his fair paintings? They are to us no more than mere decorations whose origin is long gone and unlikely to come back. They are little but the men and women of Mr. Gainsborough. He imprisoned their spirit in the crux of his artifice. Now, you might say, what of others? Is Mr. Constable a murderer because he painted an empty landscape, Nature’s finest gift? Mais bien sur! Mr. Constable is no frivolous artist, sir, and his beautiful strokes are enough reason to see that this man has the bloody instinct to kill life itself. To create a painting so great, our own pitiful lives are destroyed by its sheer beauty. His gift, what the French name genie, is his fatal blade. He loves Nature sacrilegiously, thus, he kills it. I shall conclude with a brief indulgence, which I could not forebear to disclose. As we are vastly familiar, Mr Wordsworth, whose worthy acquaintance I had the pleasure of making, wrote a fine poem which included the line “we murder to dissect.” We are free to express doubt whether we dispute Mr Wordsworth’s suggestion that Art and Science are but barren leaves, yet the Lake poet’s words are wise as pearls. This, sir, is the age of murder. Its muse is Envy and its weapon is Avarice. State and gravity are trivial affairs in face of its design, and the pre-destination it charted is in a lock. Art is men’s tool of revenge against the life which has rendered him very helpless and very wretched. The false wit of Mr. Daggers thereof is mere noise for us to resist as seamen and sea-farers – who for undisclosed reasons are well-acquainted with the concept of murder – ought resist the temptation to drink.

by Job Miller

The University does not support the change we desire. It is all too willing to maintain its fiscal investments in the economy of exploitation and destruction that the current world-system thrives upon. The administrators buckle and bend to open up campuses to the hyper-policing and forms of control so essential to neoliberalism. This is not new; the collusion of the University with the war machine can be traced at every point of the last century, from the gladhanding of the Department of Defense to the campus-infiltration of the CIA.

I am suspicious that the practices we take up as scholars, teachers, and critics in the University cannot help but bolster the very system which has oppressed us. In many moments this happens against our will, of course; but what I want to emphasize is how our investment in the University makes us complicit in its machinery of subtler repressions. Too often we allow the University to transform our thinking and desire by determining our relation to the text, to art and its inherent capacity to generate resistance. By overvaluing the University, even when it is assailed by reaction, we ignore the sinister constraints that it imposes on all of us.

I spent several years pursuing a PhD at Columbia. I spent much of that time turning in assignments far too late and of rather poor quality. It was here that my suspicion solidified that the University had no capacity to facilitate upheaval, none of the incendiary potential necessary for the dominant order to be unmade. As a teacher, I felt that the majority of my work merely taught students a set of analytical tools that could be used to blunt what was truly radical or destabilizing. Teaching George Jackson is fine and dandy, but I don’t really give a fuck if some private equity kid feels a little guilt as they plow forward in their career of exploitation and global dispossession. Worse was that I became convinced that teaching these texts became a vaccine against students’ capacity to be disrupted. Against all my intentions, such classes served to insulate these students from the world around them. We must face the University’s awesome power to invert our best intentions, to steer the content of even the most radical class into a pro forma fulfillment of the credentialed and the chosen. To ignore this process is a weakness that has rendered much of our critical work fangless, inherently flawed.

As a student at Columbia my frustration thickened. The place was afflicted by a rampant competitiveness that resulted in a space hostile to those fragile ideas which require delicate nuance to be enunciated. When we orient ourselves to the text with the crushing pressure of publication we develop a relationship to the text that is neither generative nor made in good faith. The command to write, when we have not spent enough time being humble before a text, shuts down the potential for it to overwhelm us. Then mindlessly we parrot this same demand to students who are not given enough time to consider what it is they begin to chew up and regurgitate. It is no wonder that AI becomes a viable response to this demand to produce at all costs. There is a warped relation to the text that speaks only of the fulfillment of an economic epistemology of value and exploitation. Is overwhelming ecstasy and terror not our original relation to art? Is this not the basis for our desire? Is this not what reminds us, despite the pain it brings, that the world is not as full as it could be? Instead we are driven by the pressures of the academy to perform the song and dance of “mastery.” This need to make everything not merely useful but marketable carries within it the rancid stench of double exploitation—wherein the text and ourselves are mangled. Thus when we are grinding away for the University we become merely the forerunners of the machine which seeks to make all things searchable; we become spinners of terms, crafters of keywords. It is such an unpleasantly disdainful task, a supremely silly game to play. Even those that don’t get caught up immediately are quickly digested by those who come after into fodder for the competitive-class to engorge upon. It may sound despondent to understand our work as hurrying the commodification of what is radical, but should we not face the truth of it? We are living in a time of defeat. The strategies of consumption and commodification reach deeper at every moment into the bodies of resistance. We have not intellectualized our way out. It is dark, and we are much in need of hope.

When I started out at community college I did not know what I wanted to study. I did not know terms or theory. But I did have humility and a burning desire to speak. I sensed a secret way of knowing that made me ache when I read something which was greater than myself, a sensation that made me bend before it. I possessed a certain orientation as the result of growing up poor, and of experiencing the pain of loss and the frustration of helplessness in adolescence. But I also knew the love that comes as the last resort—when there is nothing left to give piecemeal and when to give anything at all is to give everything. The glimpses available in reading grew into the conviction of study. It was not enough to have felt mere moments of liberation. It became necessary to inhabit the text as a space of refuge—as a location from which to imagine the terror and freedom beyond horizons which I had not yet known existed. Study was an act that breathed life into me as it offered a vision of the future which was no longer rooted in what job or career or path to wealth might be in store, but announced success in the form of a new world wherein my labor was returned to me, and in the joy of chasing the questions of what it means to live expanded. It was a difficult task to hold onto this conviction even as it was the only reason I could manage to write anything insightful. Even on this lower plane of academic prestige the models of study were afflicted by those too scared to admit that the task of study is irruptive. I desired recognition. I desired the aristocratic flair and grace of the language which spread itself across so much of what is written. It was difficult to know what the academy would want me to forfeit. So much of my engagement with the University was a sweet freedom from what seemed to limit me. Poverty seemed to be washed off from me as I displayed a certain mastery of the texts around me. These are the devastating trappings that became heavier the further I moved along the line of professionalism. Though the absurdity of studying literature at community college cannot be discounted, sharing in a working-class desire to do something that had no practical elaboration had its small joys. This study was not desperate to prove its value. It found its reward in the text; in sharing it. It demanded all and the reward was in shifting moments a glimpse of freedom and beauty. It was hope for something more.

Others find this absurdity of study from differing positions. This is what drives us to read. It connects us. It is what we share, but also what turns around and elaborates our difference, an individuating force, an expression of becoming that can only announce itself as the specific. This willingness and compulsion to risk it all fosters a relationship to the text that is on a radically different plane than that of the exploitative use-based commodity, desperate in its grasp for mastery. Of course this isn’t exclusive or a secret—it just requires true risk. And this risk means also risking one’s place in the academy, that machine of consumption and nullification. The University does not foster the space for this risky relation to the text, to study, to each other: we must look beyond it.

This is the reason for the titular question. Do we need to imagine its end? Do we need to imagine a different relation to each other? What does it look like to study trenchantly outside of its limitations and motivations? We need relief from this ugliness. We need to collect ourselves. We need to remember that we read because literature, art, reveals a desire beyond what the forces of order tell us we have. Do we read and study to publish? To gain postdoc positions? To secure tenure track jobs? To show how much we control the text? We have been trained to forget how far we reach, how unstable we are. It is a goddamn shame to read to produce criticism, etc., which has as its goal the opposite, namely, to make everything extra legible so that we learn and then teach how to avoid that messy sticky turmoil which is why we read in the first place. Many within the University are susceptible to its trappings. All that they engage with suffers from banality and stupidity. They can not articulate anything interesting. They cannot see past the walls meant to keep the rabble out. But what if we are the rabble let in accidentally? An undercommons is fine, but I would have much much more. We must remember this is not for us. We must remember that we desire something else entirely.

In the waiting room
we sit.
Rough upholstery
scratching our bare legs
The clock resoundingly ticking
as the minutes drag by.
Waiting to be seen.
Do you view us
as a whole
or as individuals?
Are we only a copay,
an appointment to be kept?
Red, and yellow, black and white
we are precious in HIS sight.
Our stories can aid
your understanding of us.
It is not just about the symptoms
our symptoms,
but also about the pain
our pain,
Physically
Emotionally
Spiritually.
It is about where we have been
which should not be negated.
So I will
take a number,
wait in line,
as I reflect on who I am
and pray that you see me,
the person
not just the problem.
